verses.text: Jacob lived in the land of his father’s travels, in the land of Canaan.

This is the history of the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. Joseph brought an evil report of them to their father.
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a coat of many colors.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.
Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers, and they hated him all the more.
He said to them, “Please hear this dream which I have dreamed:
for behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves came around, and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers said to him, “Will you indeed reign over us? Or will you indeed have dominion over us?” They hated him all the more for his dreams and for his words.
He dreamed yet another dream, and told it to his brothers, and said, “Behold, I have dreamed yet another dream: and behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me.”

He told it to his father and to his brothers. His father rebuked him, and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Will I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves down to you to the earth?”
His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.
His brothers went to feed their father’s flock in Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Aren’t your brothers feeding the flock in Shechem? Come, and I will send you to them.” He said to him, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “Go now, see whether it is well with your brothers, and well with the flock; and bring me word again.” So he sent him out of the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A certain man found him, and behold, he was wandering in the field. The man asked him, “What are you looking for?”
He said, “I am looking for my brothers. Tell me, please, where they are feeding the flock.”
The man said, “They have left here, for I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” Joseph went after his brothers, and found them in Dothan.
They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him.
They said to one another, “Behold, this dreamer comes.
Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
Reuben heard it, and delivered him out of their hand, and said, “Let’s not take his life.”
Reuben said to them, “Shed no blood. Throw him into this pit that is in the wilderness, but lay no hand on him” — that he might deliver him out of their hand, to restore him to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his coat, the coat of many colors that was on him;
and they took him, and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty. There was no water in it.

They sat down to eat bread, and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites was coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing spices and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?
Come, and let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not let our hand be on him; for he is our brother, our flesh.” His brothers listened to him.
Midianites who were merchants passed by, and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They brought Joseph into Egypt.
Reuben returned to the pit; and saw that Joseph wasn’t in the pit; and he tore his clothes.
He returned to his brothers, and said, “The child is no more; and I, where will I go?”
They took Joseph’s coat, and killed a male goat, and dipped the coat in the blood.
They took the coat of many colors, and they brought it to their father, and said, “We have found this. Examine it, now, whether it is your son’s coat or not.”
He recognized it, and said, “It is my son’s coat. An evil animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.”
Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days.
All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “For I will go down to Sheol  to my son mourning.” His father wept for him.
The Midianites sold him into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard.

footnotes.content: Jacob settles down in the land of Canaan, the very land promised to his fathers, yet he still lives as a sojourner. I have learned that the Lord's promises may find us dwelling in a place, but our hearts are meant to look beyond it to the God who gave it. Even in a land of promise, there is still groaning, for our true rest is only in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We meet Joseph as a seventeen-year-old boy tending sheep with his brothers, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah. It is a small thing that he brings an evil report to Jacob, but the Lord often takes notice of a boy's faithfulness long before others do. May the God who sees even the quiet act of honesty have mercy on a young heart like Joseph's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel loves Joseph more than all his children, for he is the son of his old age, and he makes him a coat of many colors. I have seen how a father's love is a beautiful gift, but when it is unevenly shown, it can become a snare to those who receive it and those who are passed by. The true Coat of Righteousness is not earned by favoritism, but freely given by our elder Brother, Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's brothers see their father's love, and hatred takes root in their hearts until they cannot even speak peaceably to him. Sin is like that: it begins by looking with envy, and before long it robs us of the simplest kindness of a brotherly word. How much we need the grace of Jesus, who speaks peace to us when our hatred has made us enemies of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph dreams, and tells his brothers the dream, and their hatred only grows all the more. I have noticed that when God gives a glimpse of His purposes to a young soul, the flesh often bristles at it. Yet the Lord who gives the dream is already faithful to bring it to pass in His own time, though the road be long.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph gently says, 'Please hear this dream which I have dreamed.' There is no arrogance in the words of a boy telling what he saw, only the wonder of one who does not yet know the weight of it. I pray we would all have such childlike wonder at the works of God, and such gentleness when we speak of them to others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dream, the sheaves of Joseph arise and stand upright, while his brothers' sheaves bow down around him. A sheaf is bound up to be brought to its place, and here the Lord shows that even the lowly will be gathered under His purpose. One day every knee shall bow to the true and greater Joseph, Jesus Christ, and every tongue confess that He is Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers bristle with pride and ask, 'Will you indeed reign over us?' Their question reveals their hearts more than Joseph's dream ever could. It is a sad thing when God's promise provokes rebellion in us, but it is our great mercy that Jesus reigns not by force of our worth, but by the mercy of His cross to save rebels like us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph dreams yet another dream, and this time the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bow down to him. The Lord is gracious to repeat His word when our faith is slow to receive it. Even so, Joseph does not yet see that the path to the bowing will be the path of the pit and the prison, a path that points us to our Savior who first humbled Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph tells the dream to his father and his brothers, and Jacob rebukes him with the question of whether they would all bow down. Yet Scripture tells us Jacob keeps this saying in mind, showing a father torn between caution and wondering. I have found that the godly often wrestle in faith, holding God's word quietly in their hearts while they wait to see how He will do it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind. Two responses to the same word of God: one roots itself in envy and bears bitter fruit, the other roots itself in faith and waits upon the Lord. May the Lord grant us the latter, to treasure His promises even when we do not understand them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers go to feed their father's flock in Shechem, the same Shechem where Jacob had bought a parcel of ground and where Dinah's grief had fallen on the family. It was good pasture country, and a place already stained with memory for this household. How often the road that seems ordinary is the road the Lord uses to carry out His hidden purposes, turning an errand of shepherding into the beginning of mercy for many.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel calls Joseph and sends him to check on his brothers and the flock, and Joseph answers with the simple words, 'Here I am.' It is the same humble answer we hear from faithful servants of old. I love that Joseph goes at his father's word in love, not knowing he is going as a lamb into the midst of wolves, just as our true Shepherd once came for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob sends Joseph out of the valley of Hebron, the old covenant ground where Abraham and Isaac had pitched their tents and where Sarah lies buried, up the ridge road toward Shechem. He only asks for word of his sons' welfare and of the flock. It is a long walk from Hebron to Shechem, and longer still once Joseph is sent on to Dothan. The Lord so often uses a father's loving errand to set in motion the very path by which He will save His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A certain man finds Joseph wandering in the field, and asks him what he is looking for. How tender is the providence of God, that a stranger should meet a lost young shepherd boy in an open field. I take comfort that the God who orders the steps of Joseph also orders the steps of His people, often sending help in the form of those we do not know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph answers simply, 'I am looking for my brothers. Tell me, please, where they are feeding the flock.' There is no pride here, only a son dutifully seeking his brothers out of love. Our greater Brother, Jesus, has left the glory above and come seeking His wandering brothers and sisters, asking where we are so that He might bring us home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man tells Joseph his brothers have gone on to Dothan, a few hours north where the caravan roads crossed and the wells were reliable for watering flocks. Joseph goes after them and finds them there, still obedient, still unaware. Dothan is only a small detour in miles, but it is an enormous turning point in his life. I have learned that the Lord's detours are never mistakes, for He leads His beloved through them to mercies we cannot yet see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They see Joseph afar off, and before he comes near, they conspire against him to kill him. Hatred has ripened to the point of plotting murder, all over a coat and a dream. How desperately we need a Savior who, when His enemies drew near to kill Him, prayed for them and laid down His life willingly to save them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers say to one another, 'Behold, this dreamer comes.' What a bitter name they give the one who brought them his father's errand in love. The world has often called the people of God dreamers, but the dreams of the Lord are sure. The greatest Dreamer of all was called a madman, yet He is the wisdom and power of God for salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They resolve to kill Joseph, cast him into a pit, and lie to their father that an evil animal has devoured him. Sin loves to hide its cruelty behind a convenient story. I shudder at the hardness of their hearts, and then remember that apart from grace, my own heart is capable of the same, and that only the blood of Jesus covers such sins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben hears it and delivers Joseph out of their hand, saying, 'Let us not take his life.' There is a flicker of conscience here, a desire to spare blood. Yet Reuben does not rebuke his brothers sharply enough, and his half-measure will not stop the evil. It reminds me that partial obedience to God cannot undo the guilt of sin, only full and free pardon through Jesus can.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben urges them to throw Joseph into the pit in the wilderness with no bloodshed, intending to restore him to his father. I see a man trying to do right, but timidly, and his timidity leaves room for others to carry out their wicked plan. The Lord often uses even our feeble efforts for good, but our hope is never in Reuben's strength, it is in the faithfulness of God Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Joseph comes to his brothers, they strip him of his coat of many colors, the token of his father's love. With one act they rob him of his dignity before they ever cast him into the pit. How like our sin, to strip others of what God has given them, and how like Jesus, who was stripped of His garments for us to clothe us with His righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They take Joseph and throw him into the pit, and the pit is empty with no water in it. A dry pit is a place of utter abandonment, a tomb without burial. I cannot help but look to Jesus, cast out by men, descended into the place of the dead for us, so that those who were cast away might be brought near to God forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sit down to eat bread while Joseph is in the pit, and behold, a caravan of Ishmaelites comes from Gilead bearing spices, balm, and myrrh on their camels, going down to Egypt. In the ancient Near East this was a common trade route, but the cruelty of eating bread beside a brother in distress is almost beyond words. The Lord uses even this heathen caravan to begin the way of deliverance, showing that His purposes run through the very things men meant for evil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah speaks up and asks, 'What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?' Here the heart of sin is laid bare: not pity, but profit. I have learned to watch for that question in my own heart, for how easily I calculate the cost of obedience over the cost of love. May we learn from Jesus, who counted us His profit and gave Himself for us at infinite cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah says, 'Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not let our hand be on him, for he is our brother, our flesh.' It is a wicked appeal to kinship to justify cruelty, sparing their hands from blood while still shedding their brother's rights. Our Lord Jesus is truly our brother in flesh, and yet He willingly gave Himself up, not to be sold by us to spare us, but to be sold for us to save us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Midianite merchants draw Joseph up out of the pit and sell him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, and he is carried down to Egypt. Twenty shekels was the going price of a young slave in that world, roughly what one might pay for a working animal. It is a sobering sum for a boy sold by his own brothers. How strange and wonderful that our Redeemer was sold for thirty pieces of silver, not to become a slave in Egypt, but to become a Servant who sets His enslaved people free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben returns to the pit and sees that Joseph is not there, and he tears his clothes. Here is the grief of one who meant well but was not there in time to stop the deed. I know this sorrow all too well, but there is One who was always there, who knew all, and who in love went to the cross on purpose to rescue His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuben returns to his brothers and says, 'The child is no more; and I, where will I go?' The words of a broken man, full of guilt and helplessness. What a mercy that our guilt leads us not to despair without hope, but to the One who has already gone ahead for us and says, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brothers take Joseph's coat, kill a male goat, and dip the coat in the blood to use it as proof of their lie. They would rather cover their sin with the blood of a goat than repent of it. How different is the true Lamb of God, whose blood was not used to cover our lies, but willingly shed to wash them away forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They bring the coat of many colors to their father and say, 'We have found this. Examine it, now, whether it is your son's coat or not.' With feigned innocence they shift the burden onto Jacob, inviting him to draw his own conclusion to their lie. I have learned that a half-truth spoken in deceit is still a lie, and only the truth of the Gospel can set our consciences free.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob recognizes it and cries, 'It is my son's coat. An evil animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.' The very words his sons fed him are the words he believes, and they pierce his fatherly heart to the core. The Lord knows every false word spoken against His children, and He will one day make all things right for those who belong to His Son.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob tears his clothes, puts sackcloth on his waist, and mourns for his son many days. Tearing the garment and wearing coarse sackcloth were the customary signs of grief in that world, a public admission that something had been torn inside as well. A father's grief is deep, and here it is honest and unrestrained. I think of our heavenly Father who, for love of us, gave up His only Son to death, and who knows the fullness of grief we only taste in part.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All his sons and daughters rise up to comfort him, but he refuses to be comforted, saying he will go down to Sheol mourning for his son. As readers today hear an echo of this grief, I know there are sorrows that no human word can heal, and we are right to weep for them. Yet as of 2026-10, I give thanks that for all who belong to Jesus, death is not the end, and the God of all comfort will one day wipe every tear away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Midianites sell Joseph into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard. From the pit to the house of a captain, the road seems downward, but the Lord is going downward with Joseph to lift up His people. This is the very way of our Savior, who descended into humility and the grave so that He might raise His people up to the highest place with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
